newsitem.title: UK: Britsh Airways seeks to cut 5,000 jobs.
newsitem.headline: Britsh Airways seeks to cut 5,000 jobs.

text.p: British Airways Plc. said on Wednesday it wanted to shed 5,000 of its 49,000 British employees to make way for new recruits with different skills, as part of a major three-year restructuring campaign.

The jobs plan was unveiled by Chief Executive Robert Ayling to 300 senior managers as part of the airline's ambitious "Step Change" efficiency drive, which aims to lop one billion British pounds ($1.56 billion) from its annual cost base by 2000.
Promising that no jobs in the airline would be unaffected by the plans, he said some would be shifted to outside companies, some relocated and some ended.

British Airways said it was considering whether it was cheaper to contract out many of its ancillary operations in Britain, including check-in, baggage loading, cargo handling and some financial services.

"Some activities could be sold or subcontracted if they can be done better or more cheaply externally, with employees involved being offered jobs with the new owner, redeployed within the airline with retraining, or taking voluntary severance or early retirement," the airline said.

British Airways wants around 5,000 staff members to take voluntary severance or early retirement over the next 18 months. Ayling said this was "to create room for a huge programme of redeployment and retraining" which would also see the airline taking on about 5,000 new employees over the next three years.
Ayling said he could not rule out compulsory severences, but doesn't expect it to be a problem. He was due to present the plans to the main staff unions on Wednesday evening.

"There is no reason why their response should be anything other than positive," he told a news conference. "I do not expect wholesale job losses. Jobs will also be created, and jobs secured. We will grow and we will improve. I am committed to a strategy of investment and improved profitability."
The Transport and General Workers Union, which represents many of British Airways's cabin crew and ground service staff, declined to comment ahead of the meeting.

British Airways ranks as the biggest international carrier and one of the most profitable airlines in the world, but Ayling said it needed to improve services and cut costs if it was to fight off new competition and offset declines in average fare levels and the rising cost of handling more traffic.
